q0001: Bolgatty Palace stands on Bolgatty (Mulavukad) Island off Kochi, Kerala. The Dutch built it in 1744; it later became the home of the British Resident.
Kochi's two palace names to keep apart: Bolgatty Palace and Mattancherry (the Dutch Palace).
q0002: Orugallu, today's Warangal in Telangana, was the Kakatiya capital. Rudrama Devi, one of India's few ruling queens, governed from here.
The Kakatiya Kala Thoranam gateway of Warangal Fort sits on Telangana's state emblem.
q0003: The Human Development Index was built for UNDP in 1990 by Mahbub ul Haq, working with Amartya Sen, whose capability approach is its foundation.
HDI combines three things: a long healthy life, knowledge (schooling) and a decent standard of living (income).
q0004: Pandita Ramabai opened Sharada Sadan for widows in 1889, and her Mukti Mission counts its founding from that year; the large home at Kedgaon near Pune followed.
Other women reformers: Savitribai Phule (first girls' school, Pune, 1848), Tarabai Shinde (Stri Purush Tulana, 1882).
Some books give 1898 for the Kedgaon (Mukti) home; DSSSB's key uses 1889.
q0008: Lord Dalhousie annexed Awadh (Oudh) in February 1856 on the ground of misgovernment, not under the Doctrine of Lapse. Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was sent to Calcutta.
Awadh's annexation fed the 1857 revolt, since many Bengal Army sepoys came from Awadh.
q0009: Indian music split into the Hindustani (north) and Carnatic (south) traditions after the 13th century, when Persian and Central Asian influences reshaped northern music under the Delhi Sultanate.
Amir Khusrau (13th–14th century) is credited with shaping early Hindustani forms such as qawwali.
q0011: All three statements are right: Calcutta Madrasa (Warren Hastings, 1781), Benares Sanskrit College (Jonathan Duncan, 1791), and the Charter Act of 1813, which set aside ₹1 lakh a year for education.
Sequence: 1781 Madrasa → 1791 Sanskrit College → 1813 Charter Act → 1835 Macaulay's Minute → 1854 Wood's Despatch.
q0015: The First Five-Year Plan (1951–56), built on the Harrod–Domar model, gave top priority to agriculture and irrigation after the food shortages of Partition.
The Second Plan (1956–61, Mahalanobis model) switched the focus to heavy industry.
q0016: Regional Rural Banks were set up on 2 October 1975 on the advice of the Narasimham Working Group. Prathama Bank, Moradabad (UP), was the first.
RRB share capital: Centre 50%, sponsor bank 35%, state government 15%.
In which year were Regional Rural Banks set up in India?
q0021: Article 243R (Part IXA, added by the 74th Amendment, 1992) says all seats in a municipality are filled by direct election from territorial constituencies (wards).
The panchayat equivalent is Article 243C. Part IX = Panchayats; Part IXA = Municipalities.
q0022: Ladakh became a Union Territory without a legislature under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019; Jammu and Kashmir became a UT with one.
UTs with an elected assembly: Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir.
q0023: The 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali to the Eighth Schedule. Maithili came later, with Bodo, Dogri and Santhali, by the 92nd Amendment (2003).
The Eighth Schedule now lists 22 languages.
Which of the following languages was NOT included in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution by the 71st Amendment Act of 1992?
q0027: The 7th Amendment (1956) carried out the States Reorganisation Act: it ended the Part A/B/C/D classes, creating 14 states and 6 union territories.
The same amendment allowed one High Court to serve two or more states.
After independence, Part C states and Part D territories were constituted as union territories under the ______ Constitutional Amendment Act.
q0028: The Peninsular Plateau is edged by the narrow Western Coastal Plains along the Arabian Sea and the broader Eastern Coastal Plains along the Bay of Bengal.
The east coast is wider because big rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) build deltas there.
q0029: India's first Water Bodies Census (2018-19) counted about 24.2 lakh water bodies. Ponds were the largest share (about 59.5%), then tanks and reservoirs.
West Bengal has the most water bodies; Tamil Nadu has the most lakes; Andhra Pradesh the most tanks.
q0030: Article 351 directs the Union to promote the spread of Hindi and develop it as a medium of expression for India's composite culture.
Article 343: Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union.
q0031: A and B are correct. C is wrong: Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting. Absorbing iron is helped by Vitamin C.
The K comes from the German 'Koagulation' — clotting.
q0032: Classical music rests on swara or sur (notes), raga (melody), taal (rhythmic cycle) and laya (tempo). Devotion is a mood or theme, not a structural part.
Teentaal, the most common Hindustani taal, has 16 beats.
q0033: The Kaveri rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills of Kodagu (Coorg), Karnataka, and reaches the Bay of Bengal through Tamil Nadu.
Don't confuse it with the Godavari, which rises near Trimbakeshwar (Nashik) — also on a hill called Brahmagiri.
q0034: Articles 14–18 give equality before law, no discrimination, equal opportunity in public jobs, abolition of untouchability and abolition of titles. Equality is not absolute: reasonable classification is allowed.
Reservation under Article 16(4) is possible precisely because equality is not absolute.
q0035: Census 2011: Rajasthan had the lowest female literacy (about 52%), and Kerala the highest (about 92%).
q0036: Reducing sugars have a free aldehyde or ketone group, so they reduce mild oxidising agents such as Fehling's and Tollens' reagents. Glucose is one; sucrose is not.
Glucose turns blue Fehling's solution into a brick-red precipitate.
q0037: Turner's syndrome (45, X0) is a female with one X chromosome missing: short stature, underdeveloped ovaries, sterility.
Klinefelter's syndrome is the opposite case: a male with an extra X (47, XXY).
q0038: The Water Bodies Census 2018-19 found Tamil Nadu has the most lakes, while West Bengal has the most water bodies overall (mostly ponds).
q0039: Most Indian Buddhists are Navayana (neo-Buddhists) who followed Dr B. R. Ambedkar's mass conversion of 1956, many from Scheduled Caste communities, so the SC share among Buddhists is the highest.
Ambedkar converted to Buddhism at Nagpur's Deekshabhoomi on 14 October 1956.
q0040: Guru Bipin Singh (1918–2000) is called the father of modern Manipuri dance; he received the Kalidas Samman.
Manipuri's best-known forms: Ras Lila, and the Pung Cholom drum dance.
q0043: The National Food for Work Programme (November 2004, in 150 backward districts) was 100% centrally sponsored. It was merged into MGNREGA in 2006.
MGNREGA's funding is different: the Centre pays all unskilled wages and 75% of material costs.
q0046: Consumption (final) goods are bought by the ultimate user for direct use, like food or a shirt. Goods used to make other goods are producer or capital goods.
Flour bought by a household is a consumption good; the same flour bought by a bakery is an intermediate good.
q0048: Madan Mohan Malaviya was a founder-leader of the Hindu Mahasabha (1915), four times Congress president, and founder of Banaras Hindu University (1916).
q0050: Sir William Jones founded the Asiatic Society (of Bengal) in Calcutta in 1784 to study Asian languages, history and culture.
Jones translated Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam into English (1789).
q0051: The standing Bodhisattva found at Sarnath was carved in Mathura's red sandstone in the Kushana period and dedicated by the monk Friar Bala.
Kushana-era schools: Mathura (red sandstone, Indian style), Gandhara (grey schist, Greek-influenced), Amaravati (white marble).
q0053: The Green Revolution of the mid-1960s was driven by high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, especially wheat and rice, used with fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation.
M. S. Swaminathan is called the father of India's Green Revolution; Norman Borlaug developed the Mexican dwarf wheat.
q0054: At the Battle of Ghaghra (1529) in Bihar, Babur defeated the Afghan chiefs of eastern India led by Mahmud Lodi. It was his last major battle.
Babur's big three: Panipat 1526 (Ibrahim Lodi), Khanwa 1527 (Rana Sanga), Chanderi 1528 (Medini Rai).
q0055: Cobb and Douglas first tested their production function on data for the whole US manufacturing industry (1899–1922).
Form: Q = A·L^a·K^b, where L is labour and K is capital.
q0057: The Paika Rebellion of 1817 broke out in Khurda, Orissa, led by Bakshi Jagabandhu, against East India Company rule and its land revenue policy.
Odisha asks for it to be called the 'First War of Independence', forty years before 1857.
q0058: Muhammad bin Tughlaq appointed amiran-i-sada (commanders over groups of a hundred villages) to run the Deccan after shifting his capital to Daulatabad.
Their revolt later led to the founding of the Bahmani kingdom (1347).
q0059: The Sen Index (Amartya Sen, 1976) combines how many people are poor, how far below the line they are, and inequality among the poor.
Headcount ratio counts the poor; the poverty gap measures how far below the line they fall.
Strictly, averaging the squared poverty gap is the Foster–Greer–Thorbecke (P2) measure; DSSSB's key marks the Sen Index.
q0061: The North Temperate Zone lies between the Tropic of Cancer (23½°N) and the Arctic Circle (66½°N).
Torrid zone: between the two Tropics. Frigid zones: beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles.
Which of the following statements best describes the position of the North Temperate Zone?
q0065: The Krishna empties into the Bay of Bengal directly; the Kosi reaches it through the Ganga. Every other pair has a river that drains to the Arabian Sea or into the Ganga.
West-flowing rivers to the Arabian Sea: Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati.
The Kosi is a tributary of the Ganga, so this pair is correct only in the sense of draining to the Bay of Bengal.
Select the correct pair of rivers which flow into the Bay of Bengal.
q0066: Kankar are calcareous (lime) nodules found in the older alluvium of the Ganga plains, in the drier upper parts away from the fresh floodplains.
Bhangar = older alluvium away from rivers; khadar = new alluvium on the floodplains.
q0068: Nepal's Terai is the fertile, low-lying strip along the Indian border; roughly half of Nepal's people live there.
Terai lies south of the Bhabar belt at the foot of the Himalayas, where streams re-emerge as marshy land.
q0069: The Bagh Caves (Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh) are nine rock-cut Buddhist monasteries from the Gupta period, famous for murals similar to Ajanta's.
Buddhist rock-cut sites: Ajanta, Bagh, Karla, Bhaja, Kanheri. Ellora mixes Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves.
The Bagh Caves are considered important examples of which architectural tradition?
q0073: India's traditional coastline figure, mainland plus islands, is 7,516.6 km (about 7,517 km), touching 9 states and 4 UTs.
Gujarat has the longest mainland coastline.
A 2023-24 re-measurement with new methods puts the coastline at 11,098 km; exam keys set before that use 7,517 km.
What is the total length of the coastline of India's mainland and island groups?
q0075: Under Article 74 the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister, including when summoning and proroguing Parliament or dissolving the Lok Sabha.
Article 85 is the summon/prorogue/dissolve power; the advice is binding after the 42nd and 44th Amendments.
q0076: The Rajya Sabha is the Council of States, the upper house that represents the states and UTs; it is a permanent body that is never dissolved.
Lok Sabha = House of the People. One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every two years.
q0077: Mallika Sarabhai is a noted exponent of Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam and runs the Darpana Academy in Ahmedabad, founded by her mother Mrinalini Sarabhai.
Kuchipudi comes from Andhra Pradesh; Bharatanatyam from Tamil Nadu.
q0078: WHO and UNICEF recommend zinc, with ORS, for children with diarrhoea, and for severely malnourished children, because zinc shortens the illness and helps recovery.
Standard advice: ORS plus 10–14 days of zinc for childhood diarrhoea.
q0079: Malayalam is the main language of Kerala and Kannada of Karnataka. Both are recognised classical languages (Kannada 2008, Malayalam 2013).
Telugu was recognised along with Kannada in 2008.
q0080: Cantonment Boards run civic affairs in military cantonments and are under the Ministry of Defence, now under the Cantonments Act, 2006.
India has 62 notified cantonments; the Station Commander usually heads the board.
q0084: English is Meghalaya's official language, and Khasi and Garo are associate official languages under the Meghalaya State Language Act, 2005.
Meghalaya's three hill regions are named after its peoples: Khasi, Garo and Jaintia Hills.
Which of the following can be used as official languages in the Indian state of Meghalaya?
q0085: After the Chola decline in the 13th century, the Pandyas of Madurai became the leading Tamil power, especially under Jatavarman Sundara Pandya.
Marco Polo visited the Pandya kingdom in the 1290s.
After the fall of the Cholas, which of the following was the leading Tamil dynasty?
q0086: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad started Al-Hilal (1912) to spread nationalist politics among Muslims; because it did, the British suppressed it in 1914. So A and R are both true and R explains A.
Azad's next paper, Al-Balagh, was also banned, and he was interned in Ranchi.
Assertion (A): The British government suppressed the publication of Al-Hilal. Reason (R): It began to advocate nationalist politics.
q0087: Humayun-nama was written by Gulbadan Begum, Humayun's sister, at Akbar's request.
Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari: Abul Fazl. Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi): Babur himself, in Turki.
q0088: Using resources wisely so future generations can also meet their needs is conservation, which is the idea behind sustainable development.
The definition comes from the Brundtland Commission's report 'Our Common Future' (1987).

Which environmental concept best describes the responsible and ethical use of resources to meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs?
q0089: Famine commissions in order: Campbell (1866, Orissa famine), Strachey (1880), Lyall (1898), MacDonnell (1901).
The Strachey Commission led to the first Famine Code (1883).
Arrange the following famine commissions formed during the British period in the order of their establishment.
q0090: Indian cotton and silk textiles, metalwork and gem crafts sold worldwide before British rule because of their very high craftsmanship.
Dhaka muslin and Masulipatnam chintz were prized in Europe.
India's handicraft industries, particularly cotton and silk textiles, metalwork and precious stone crafts, enjoyed a global market before the arrival of the British because:
q0091: Qutbuddin Aibak was called 'Lakh Baksh' (giver of lakhs) for his generosity.
He began the Qutub Minar and built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in Delhi; he died falling from a horse playing chaugan (polo).
Who among the following Delhi Sultans was called 'Lakh Baksh' because of his generosity?
q0092: The Victoria Memorial in Kolkata (1906–1921), in white Makrana marble, is a leading example of British colonial (Indo-Saracenic) architecture.
Other colonial landmarks: Gateway of India (Mumbai), Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Rashtrapati Bhavan (Lutyens).
Which of the following is a prominent example of British colonial architecture in India?
q0093: Chronic poor: people who are always poor, together with those usually poor who occasionally have a little more money, such as casual workers.
Churning poor move in and out of poverty; occasionally poor are rich most of the time but may sometimes fall below the line.
People who are always poor and the people who are usually poor but may sometimes have a little more money (example: casual workers) are grouped together as __________.
q0094: Sanskrit was declared a classical language in 2005, the second after Tamil (2004).
Order: Tamil 2004, Sanskrit 2005, Telugu and Kannada 2008, Malayalam 2013, Odia 2014; Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali in 2024.
In which year was Sanskrit declared a classical language of India?
q0101: Article 14: the State shall not deny any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws within India.
Equality before law comes from British law; equal protection of laws comes from the US Constitution.
Which Article of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Equality Before Law and Equal Protection of Laws?
q0102: The Geological Survey of India (1851) has its headquarters in Kolkata. The other pairs are wrong: ONGC is in New Delhi (registered at Dehradun), MECL in Nagpur, NMDC in Hyderabad.
GSI was set up mainly to find coal for the railways.
Which of the following pairs of agencies involved in mineral exploration and their headquarters is correct?
q0103: Andaman and Nicobar → Calcutta High Court; Daman and Diu → Bombay High Court; Lakshadweep → Kerala High Court; Puducherry → Madras High Court.
Delhi is the only UT with its own High Court (1966); Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share one.

Match the Union Territories with their judiciaries: a. Andaman and Nicobar Islands, b. Daman and Diu, c. Lakshadweep, d. Puducherry — with i. Bombay High Court, ii. Calcutta High Court, iii. Madras High Court, iv. Kerala High Court.
q0104: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority from Rakhine State in Myanmar; since 2017 about a million have fled to Bangladesh.
Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh holds the world's largest refugee camp.
In which country are the Rohingya people, an ethnic minority, primarily located?
q0105: The North Cachar Hills district (now Dima Hasao) of Assam has an autonomous district council under the Sixth Schedule.
Sixth Schedule states: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.
The North Cachar Hills district is an autonomous district council of which state?
q0106: Part VIII (Articles 239–242) deals with Union Territories; each UT is run by the President through an administrator.
Article 239AA (69th Amendment, 1991) gives Delhi its special status as the National Capital Territory.
Administration of Union Territories is mentioned in which of the following Parts of the Constitution of India?
q0107: Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma is its matrix and it carries red cells, white cells and platelets.
Other connective tissues: bone, cartilage, tendon, ligament, adipose (fat).
What type of tissue is blood made up of?
q0108: Seasons exist because Earth's axis is tilted 23½°. With no tilt, each place would get the same sun angle all year, so seasons would almost disappear.
That is why the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn sit at 23½° north and south.
If the Earth's axis were not tilted, what change would most likely occur regarding the temperature pattern?
q0109: Article 123 lets the President issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session; an ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved.
Governors have the same power for states under Article 213.
Who among the following has the power to promulgate ordinances during the recess of Parliament, as per Article 123?
q0110: Both are right: the Ghaghara rises in the glaciers of Mapchachungo, and collects the Tila, Seti and Beri before leaving the mountains at Shishapani.
The Ghaghara joins the Ganga near Chhapra in Bihar.
Read the statements regarding the Ghaghara river. A. It originates from the glaciers of Mapchachungo. B. Tila, Seti and Beri are tributaries of the Ghaghara.
q0111: Article 214 says there shall be a High Court for each state; Article 231 lets Parliament set up one common High Court for two or more states.
According to the Constitution of India, which Article specifies the provision for the establishment of a High Court in each state?
q0112: The Great Stupa at Sanchi has four elaborately carved toranas (gateways), one at each cardinal direction, added in the 1st century BCE.
Ashoka commissioned the original brick stupa in the 3rd century BCE.
The Sanchi Stupa has how many profusely carved ornamental gateways?
q0113: The Koderma belt of Jharkhand holds India's biggest mica reserves; mica is used in electrical and electronic insulation.
Other mica areas: Nellore (Andhra Pradesh) and Bhilwara–Ajmer (Rajasthan).
India has the biggest reserve of _______ in the Koderma district of Jharkhand.
q0114: The Citizenship Act, 1955 allows citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory. Investment is not a route.
It can be lost by renunciation, termination or deprivation.
Which of the following is NOT a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship?
q0115: The Right to Information Act was passed in 2005, when Dr Manmohan Singh was Prime Minister; it came fully into force on 12 October 2005.
The President at the time was Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam.
Who among the following was the Prime Minister of India when the Right to Information Bill was passed in Parliament?
q0116: Census 2011: Muslims were the largest religious minority, about 14.2% of the population.
Which religious community forms the largest minority group in India, according to the 2011 Census?
q0117: Maithili, with Bodo, Dogri and Santhali, was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Amendment Act of 2003, which came into force in January 2004.
Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali had been added earlier, in 1992.
Which of the following languages was added to the Eighth Schedule in 2004?
q0118: Bacteria (kingdom Monera) come in shapes such as cocci (round), bacilli (rods), vibrio (comma) and spirilla (spiral). A heterocyst is a nitrogen-fixing cell in some cyanobacteria, not a shape.
Identify the shape which is NOT found in the kingdom Monera.
q0119: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's orbit, so at most full moons the Moon passes above or below Earth's shadow. An eclipse happens only near the nodes.
A lunar eclipse can happen only at full moon; a solar eclipse only at new moon.
Why does a lunar eclipse NOT occur every full moon?
q0120: From outside in, a root cross-section shows epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, then the vascular tissue (xylem and phloem).
Lateral roots grow from the pericycle.
Identify the correct sequence from the outer to the inner side in the transverse section of a plant root.
q0121: Vijayalaya founded the imperial Chola line around 850 CE by capturing Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars.
Greatest Cholas: Rajaraja I (Brihadeeswara Temple) and Rajendra I (Gangaikondacholapuram).
q0122: Raja Ram Mohan Roy is called the Father of the Indian Renaissance; he founded the Brahmo Sabha (1828) and campaigned against sati, abolished in 1829.
The Mughal emperor Akbar II gave him the title 'Raja'.
q0123: The Kyoto Protocol (adopted 1997, in force 2005) set binding greenhouse-gas cuts for developed countries under the UNFCCC.
The Paris Agreement (2015) replaced it with pledges from all countries.
q0124: CRR is the share of deposits a bank must keep with the RBI as cash. 15% of ₹10,000 crore = ₹1,500 crore.
SLR is different: that share is kept in liquid assets such as government securities.
q0125: The present Jagannath Temple at Puri was built in the 12th century by Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva of the Eastern Ganga dynasty.
Puri is one of the four Char Dham; its Rath Yatra takes place in Ashadha (June–July).
In which of the following centuries was the Jagannath temple built?
q0129: Import substitution means producing at home the goods the country used to import, usually behind tariffs, to save foreign exchange and build industry.
India followed it from the Second Plan until the 1991 reforms.
The policy of import substitution promotes ______.
q0138: A positive externality is a benefit that spills over to others without payment, like a beekeeper's bees pollinating a neighbour's orchard.
A negative externality is a cost imposed on others, such as factory smoke.
q0140: Ajit Singh (Bhagat Singh's uncle) founded the Bharat Mata Society in Punjab in 1907, with Sufi Amba Prasad, to oppose the colonisation laws.
Ajit Singh and Lala Lajpat Rai were deported to Mandalay in 1907.
q0141: Near the equator the Sun's rays fall almost vertically, so the same energy is concentrated on a smaller area. That makes equatorial regions warmer.
Near the poles the rays are slanting and spread over a larger area.
q0142: Citizenship is in Articles 5–11, Part II of the Constitution; Parliament used Article 11 to pass the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Article 5: citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
q0143: Dhrupad is the oldest surviving Hindustani vocal style — slow, grave and meditative, and usually devotional.
Masters: Tansen and the Dagar family. Khayal, thumri and tappa are later and lighter.
q0144: The Central Highlands lie north of the Narmada and cover most of the Malwa Plateau; the Deccan Plateau lies south of the Narmada.
Rivers of the Central Highlands (Chambal, Betwa, Ken) flow north-east.
q0145: India's first Water Bodies Census was carried out in 2018-19 with the 6th Minor Irrigation Census; the report came out in 2023.
It counted about 24.2 lakh water bodies.
In which of the following years was India's first water bodies census conducted?
q0149: The Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur, built by Rajaraja Chola I (completed 1010 CE), is dedicated to Lord Shiva.
It is part of the UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples' with Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram.
The Brihadeeswara Temple in Thanjavur is primarily dedicated to which Hindu deity?
q0150: The Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur has a huge monolithic Nandi and a vimana about 66 m tall, among the tallest temple towers of its age.
The capstone at the top of the vimana is said to weigh about 25 tonnes.
q0151: The framers gave the Union strong powers mainly to protect India's unity and integrity after Partition and the integration of the princely states.
That is why India is called a 'Union of States' with a strong centre.
q0152: Auxin causes cell elongation, which makes shoots bend towards light (phototropism); it also promotes rooting and apical dominance.
Gibberellin: stem lengthening. Cytokinin: cell division. Abscisic acid: dormancy, the stress hormone. Ethylene: fruit ripening.
q0153: The 1991 Census tried specially to record women's unpaid work on family farms and in family enterprises, which earlier censuses had largely missed.
Census 2011 was India's 15th census and the 7th after Independence.
q0154: In summer the ITCZ moves north with the overhead Sun. Over India it reaches about 20–25°N (the monsoon trough), pulling in the south-west monsoon.
In winter it moves south of the equator.
q0155: Part II of the Constitution (Articles 5–11) deals with citizenship.
Part III = Fundamental Rights; Part IV = Directive Principles; Part IVA = Fundamental Duties.
q0156: The human brain has about 86 billion neurons.
The cerebellum holds most of them, although the cerebrum is larger.
q0157: Puducherry has a Legislative Assembly (Government of Union Territories Act, 1963), as do Delhi and Jammu and Kashmir.
Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, and Andaman and Nicobar have no legislature.
q0158: Under Article 200 a Governor can reserve a state bill for the President; under Article 201 the President may then assent or withhold assent.
Money bills reserved for the President cannot be returned to the state legislature for reconsideration.
q0159: The Victoria Memorial in Kolkata is the city's best-known colonial monument, designed by William Emerson.
Basilica of Bom Jesus is in Goa; Gateway of India is in Mumbai.
q0160: The genetic code is a triplet: three bases make one codon. It is nearly universal and degenerate (several codons for one amino acid), and AUG both codes methionine and starts translation.
64 codons in all: 61 code for amino acids, 3 are stop codons.
q0161: Sonal Mansingh, a leading Odissi and Bharatanatyam dancer, received the Padma Bhushan (1992), the Padma Vibhushan (2003) and Madhya Pradesh's Kalidas Samman.
She was nominated to the Rajya Sabha in 2018.
The question says Kathak and Bharatanatyam; she is best known for Odissi and Bharatanatyam. DSSSB's answer, Sonal Mansingh, still stands.
q0162: Matangini Hazra, called 'Gandhi Buri' (old lady Gandhi), was shot dead at 73 while leading a Quit India procession at Tamluk, Bengal, in 1942.
Kanaklata Barua of Assam was also shot while carrying the flag in 1942, at 17.
q0163: Literacy rate is the standard indicator of educational attainment, and one of the inputs of the Human Development Index.
Infant mortality and life expectancy measure health; GDP measures output.
q0166: The early Cholas of Uraiyur rose as feudatories of the Pallavas of Kanchi; Vijayalaya took Thanjavur around 850 CE.
The Cholas later absorbed Pallava territory under Aditya I.
q0167: The 1857 revolt began with the mutiny of sepoys at Meerut on 10 May 1857; they marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor.
Mangal Pandey's attack at Barrackpore (29 March 1857) came earlier but stayed an isolated act.
q0168: Mecca Masjid is in Hyderabad, begun under Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in 1617. Mehrangarh is in Jodhpur, Hawa Mahal in Jaipur, and Golconda Fort in Hyderabad.
Gol Gumbaz is the famous monument of Bijapur.
q0169: Hyder Ali of Mysore fought the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–69), which ended with the Treaty of Madras.
Tipu Sultan died in the Fourth War (1799) at Srirangapatna.
q0172: MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of wage employment a year to every rural household whose adults volunteer for unskilled manual work.
If work is not given within 15 days of applying, an unemployment allowance is due.
q0176: Spread (net interest margin) = lending rate minus deposit rate; it is the bank's main source of profit.
Lend at 10% and pay 6% on deposits: the spread is 4%.
q0177: Over-indebtedness is a major MFI problem: poor borrowers take several loans from different lenders and then cannot repay.
The 2010 Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis was driven by over-indebtedness.

Dr Rajendra Prasad is the only President elected twice.

q0226: The Pashtuns are the largest ethnic group of Afghanistan and are also numerous in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
